# Card 004 — Modern infantry small arms for US, ARVN and RF/PF: M4A1 URG-I with Aimpoint CompM5, M110A2 squad marksman rifle, M249 squad automatic weapon

*Memorandum 004 · status complete · full record: memos/004/ · generated by fie.py*

## P004a · M4A1 carbine with the Upper Receiver Group – Improved (URG-I: Geissele Automatics upper, Daniel Defense 14.5-inch 1:7 barrel, mid-length gas, Mk16 13.5-inch M-LOK rail, SureFire SF4P flash hider) and Aimpoint CompM5 2 MOA red-dot sight, firing M855A1 5.56mm, 2026 configuration
All rifles and carbines of US forces and the RVNAF, and all RF/PF [U]: a first increment of about 600,000 carbines and sights in 1964, rising to about 1.7–1.9 million cumulative by 1972 [E: RVNAF 514,000 in 1964 and about 1,048,000 in 1971–72 per S9, US strength rising to about 540,000 at peak, plus a 10% float] · spaces ~250 [E: about 120 new-equipment training spaces in the first year, about 80 small-arms and optics repair technicians at the depots, and about 50 added small-arms advisers to the RF/PF training centres; no troop ceiling is set, but each space still costs] · arrives 1964-01-01 · SECURE, FIX, ADVISE, SUSTAIN · ground

**Key figures.**
- M4A1 with URG-I: Geissele upper, Daniel Defense 14.5-inch 1:7 barrel, mid-length gas, Mk16 13.5-inch M-LOK rail, SF4P flash hider [M004·S1] [M004·S2]
- Aimpoint CompM5: 1x, 2 MOA, 148 g, 50,000 hours on one battery, submersible to 45 m [M004·S3]
- M855A1: penetrates 3/8-inch steel at about 400 m; fielded June 2010 [M004·S10]
- Effective range about 500 m point, 600 m area; ready weight about 4.1 kg loaded [E: Army figures for the 14.5-inch M4A1 and component weights]
- First increment about 600,000 carbines in 1964; about 1.7–1.9 million cumulative by 1972 [E: RVNAF 514,000 in 1964 and 1,048,000 in 1971–72 per S9, US strength, 10% float]
- Historical baseline: M16 to ARVN infantry by mid-1968 and to the territorials by end-1969; AK-47 in enemy hands from 1964 [M004·S7]
- Engagements in this country at about 10–30 m, almost never beyond 100 m [M004·S8]
- First-year 5.56mm for the RVNAF about 300–400 million rounds, about 5,000 tonnes packed [E: issue, basic load, qualification and expenditure]
- US spaces about 250 [E: training, repair and RF/PF advisers]

**Negative specification.** **It does not find the enemy.** A rifle acts only in a contact, and the enemy still chooses most contacts [E: the historical record of who initiated engagements]; the main force under the canopy and the VCI inside the hamlet are exactly as hard to find as before. **It does not make a unit go out at night**, stay at its post after dark, or accept a fight its commander would avoid: whether the Popular Forces platoon sleeps in the hamlet or in the district town is a matter of leadership and pay. **It is not night vision**: the red dot can be seen in the dark, but the target must be seen too, and the force has no night-vision devices in 1964. **It does not outrange the enemy in the jungle**, where fights are at 10–30 metres. **It does not break a bunker.** **It does not make the RVNAF more self-sufficient**: every round is American. **It does not arm the National Police, the Police Field Force, the CIDG or the allied contingents.** Every outpost that falls gives the Front modern carbines, sights that run five years on a battery, and 5.56mm.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the main force and the local force the firepower advantage that the AK-47 gave them over the ARVN, the Regional Forces and the Popular Forces from 1964 until those forces received the M16 in 1968–69. It denies the Front's propaganda the outgunned government soldier, and it denies the attacking company the outpost whose garrison has eight-round Garands and carbines.

**Verdict.** This is a real improvement, concentrated where the war is decided: at night, at the wall of an outpost, in the first seconds of a contact. For the American forces it is an improvement and no more, because the M16A1 they historically carry is the same calibre and its 1967 crisis was fixable. For the ARVN infantry it closes, four years early, the firepower gap that history recorded and that ARVN soldiers felt. For the Regional and Popular Forces, who historically fought five years with carbines against AK-47s, it is the largest change: the territorials are the men who hold the hamlets at night, and an outpost that is not outgunned holds longer. What it does not do is just as plain. It does not find anyone, does not make an absent platoon present, does not touch the VCI, and every outpost lost arms the enemy with it. It improves the force inside its rung; I do not expect it to move the rung by itself.

## P004b · Knight's Armament Company M110A2 7.62mm semi-automatic rifle (20-inch free-floated match barrel, integral suppressor, 12-inch M-LOK handguard, collapsible stock) with SIG Sauer TANGO6T 1-6x24mm first-focal-plane illuminated variable-power scope, firing M118LR and M80A1 7.62mm, issued one per infantry squad as the designated marksman's rifle, 2026 configuration
One per US and ARVN infantry squad [U]: about 5,000 rifles and scopes in 1964, about 13,000 cumulative by 1972 [E: about 120 ARVN, Ranger, Airborne and Marine battalions of about 36 squads in 1964 rising to about 180 by 1972, plus up to about 112 US Army and Marine manoeuvre battalions at the 1968–69 peak, plus a 10% float] · spaces ~120 [E: marksman instructor teams of about 60 at the training centres and about 60 match-rifle and scope armourers; the marksmen themselves are squad members already counted] · arrives 1964-01-01 · FIX, SECURE, STRIKE · ground

**Key figures.**
- M110A2 (KAC): 7.62x51mm, 20-inch free-floated match barrel, integral suppressor, 10.5 lb default configuration, point targets past 1,000 m [M004·S4]
- SIG TANGO6T 1-6x24mm FFP, 30 mm tube, about 626 g, 762 Extended Range reticle, nine day and two NV illumination settings, one CR2032, IPX-8 to 20 m [M004·S5]
- Practical squad-marksman range about 600–800 m; ready weight about 6.5 kg [E: Army SDM employment and component weights]
- One per US and ARVN infantry squad [U]: about 5,000 in 1964, about 13,000 cumulative by 1972 [E: battalion and squad counts, float]
- Marksman training two to four weeks; first trained marksmen about three months after arrival [E: SDM course length and instructor pipeline]
- First-year 7.62mm about 3–6 million rounds, about half match [E: basic load and training]
- US spaces about 120 [E: instructors and armourers]

**Negative specification.** **It is not a sniper rifle in a sniper's hands.** One man in each squad, trained for weeks, using it within 600–800 m [E: squad-marksman employment]; not a hunter working alone beyond 1,000 m. **It is no help under canopy**, where the fight is at 10–30 m and the rifle is a heavy carbine with a small magazine. **It does not see at night**: the scope's illuminated reticle helps under flares and moonlight, but the force has no night-vision devices. **It works only after the marksmen are trained**, three months after the rifles arrive at the earliest. **It is a second calibre and a second ammunition line at squad level**: match 7.62mm, separately stocked. **The Regional and Popular Forces do not receive it.**

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy free movement at 300–800 m in the open [E: the marksman's practical range], where his snipers, machine gunners and leaders have historically been out of reach of the M16 and the AK alike. It denies his own snipers the uncontested ground around a firebase or an outpost, and it costs his sapper teams forming for an assault under flare light.

**Verdict.** This is a narrow tool and, in its terrain, a good one. In the Delta, the coastal plain, the paddy country and around the firebases, a trained marksman in each squad kills the enemy's leaders and gunners at ranges nobody else in the squad can reach, and the suppressor keeps him alive to do it again. Under the canopy, where much of the main-force war is fought, it does nothing a carbine does not. It depends on training the ARVN does not yet have, on squad leaders who know how to use it, and on the marksman staying alive. Its effect on the war is real and small: it improves the squad's fire where the fight is in the open, and it does not change which side chooses the fight.

**Pushes:** FIX.capability +1, ARVN.effectiveness +1 · **Depends on:** ARVN.leadership, LOG.distribution, FIND.main_force

## P004c · FN America M249 5.56mm light machine gun (PIP-standard, 465mm barrel, collapsible stock) with SIG Sauer TANGO6T 1-6x24mm scope (DWLR-556 reticle), firing linked M855A1 from 200-round pouches or STANAG magazines, at squad level in US and ARVN infantry in place of the BAR and the squad's automatic weapon, 2026 configuration
At squad level in US and ARVN infantry [U]: about 5,200 guns in 1964, about 17,000–19,000 cumulative by 1972 [E: one per ARVN squad in place of its BAR, two per Army squad and three per Marine squad in place of the fire teams' automatic rifles, on the battalion counts of P004b, plus a 10% float] · spaces ~100 [E: machine-gun instructor teams of about 40 and about 60 armourers for barrels, gas systems and feed trays; the gunners are squad members already counted] · arrives 1964-01-01 · FIX, SECURE · ground

**Key figures.**
- M249 PIP (FN America), 465 mm barrel: 7.5 kg empty, 10 kg with a 200-round pouch; cyclic 750–850, rapid 100, sustained 50 rounds a minute; 700 m point, 3,600 m maximum [M004·S6]
- Feeds linked M855A1 or STANAG magazines [M004·S6] [M004·S10]
- SIG TANGO6T 1-6x24mm with DWLR-556 reticle [M004·S5]
- One per ARVN squad, two per US Army squad, three per Marine squad [E: squad organisations]; about 5,200 in 1964, about 17,000–19,000 cumulative by 1972 [E: battalion counts, float]
- Highest stoppage rate of US small arms in the 2006 CNA survey, 30% of users [M004·S6]
- First-year linked 5.56mm about 20–30 million rounds [E: basic load, training, expenditure]
- US spaces about 100 [E: instructors and armourers]

**Negative specification.** **It is not a general-purpose machine gun.** It replaces the squad's automatic weapon, not the M60 in the platoon or company, which stays; it does not have the M60's reach and penetration [E: 7.62mm NATO against 5.56mm]. **It does not fight longer than its ammunition**: at the sustained rate of 50 rounds a minute a gun empties its gunner's load in about a quarter of an hour, and every round comes up an interdicted road. **Its stoppage record is the worst of modern US small arms in survey**; in mud and monsoon it needs cleaning. **It does not see at night.** **The Regional and Popular Forces do not receive it**: the outpost keeps its BAR.

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy's RPD-armed squads the advantage of a belt-fed gun against an ARVN squad with a 20-round BAR, and it denies the enemy assault the pause when the BAR reloads.

**Verdict.** This is the most combat-significant of the three provisions at squad level. A belt-fed gun at the centre of each ARVN squad gives it a base of fire it has never had: it can hold an enemy in contact, cover a withdrawal, break an assault on a perimeter. In a meeting engagement or an ambush, the squad that has a belt-fed gun and uses it well wins more often. It is heavy, it eats ammunition, it jams if it is not cleaned, and its gunner is the enemy's first target. It does not find the enemy or decide when the fight happens. It makes the squads that fight better at fighting, which matters every day in this war, though it is not where the war's hardest problem lies.

**Pushes:** FIX.capability +1, ARVN.effectiveness +1, LOG.distribution -1 · **Depends on:** LOG.distribution, ENEMY.engagement_control, ADVISE.leverage, PAVN.strength_south

## Employment concepts
EC004-1 the outpost wall at night · EC004-2 the zeroing round (with P001b, P002b) · EC004-3 the squad base of fire · EC004-4 the column's first minute · EC004-5 the marksman's overwatch · EC004-6 the perimeter under the flares. Abandoned: EC004-7 marksmen pooled as battalion sniper teams (no targets under canopy; squads lost overwatch; teams killed) · EC004-8 issue through the district depot (sights sold, rifles unzeroed) · EC004-9 volume of fire as doctrine (ammunition gone in a minute) · EC004-10 the squad gun to the outposts (no linked ammunition or barrels at the posts)

## Interactions
- P004a × P002a: the police post's rule requires a Popular Forces platoon beside it; the provision rearms the platoon, not the constables, and the platoon is what holds the post, so the rule and the rifle are each worth less alone
- P004a × P001b: the muster service counts carbines, sights and magazines against the soldier who holds them; the Commission follows the missing ones, and a carbine on the muster roll is harder to sell than one on a depot ledger
- P004a × P002b: the merit-selected district chief controls the territorials' ammunition; whether the outposts are resupplied or the rounds are sold is his decision
- P004a × P001a: Popular Forces recruited from titled families guard their own fields with a rifle that is not outgunned by the guerrillas who would take the land back
- P004b, P004c × P003a, P003b: none of weight; the aircraft find movement in the open and the squad weapons act in a contact at 10–30 metres, and the two are not coupled
